content: Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), also referred to as Feline AIDS, is a lentivirus that infects domestic cats globally. Approximately 11% of cats worldwide are infected with FIV, while in the United States, the prevalence is around 5%. FIV belongs to the retrovirus family, similar to feline leukemia virus (FeLV), but it is taxonomically distinct from both FeLV and feline foamy virus (FFV). FIV has been classified into five subtypes based on differences in the amino acid sequences of the viral envelope. While FIV is not a death sentence for infected cats, it is also not curable. A vaccine exists, but its effectiveness remains uncertain. The virus was first identified in 1986 in a colony of cats with a high prevalence of opportunistic infections and degenerative conditions. Since then, it has been recognized as an endemic disease in domestic cat populations worldwide. The primary mode of FIV transmission is through deep bite wounds, unlike FeLV, which spreads more easily through casual contact such as grooming or sharing water bowls. There is ongoing debate among experts about whether FIV can be transmitted through casual contact. The virus can also be transmitted via mucosal surfaces, such as those in the mouth, rectum, and vagina. FIV targets the immune system of cats in a manner similar to how human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) affects the human immune system. It infects various cell types, including CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, and macrophages. Over time, FIV leads to immune system dysfunction by depleting and exhausting T-helper (CD4+) cells. Although both FIV and HIV are lentiviruses, they are species-specific; humans cannot be infected by FIV, and cats cannot be infected by HIV. FIV is primarily transmitted through saliva, particularly via bite wounds sustained during territorial fights, often between male cats. Cats that live exclusively indoors and do not come into contact with infected cats are at a much lower risk of infection. Unfortunately, FIV-infected cats are often euthanized, but with proper care and treatment of secondary infections, they can live nearly normal lifespans. The likelihood of an FIV-infected cat transmitting the virus to other cats within the same household is very low, provided there is no fighting or biting. However, the only guaranteed way to prevent transmission is to separate infected cats from uninfected ones. The disease progresses through three stages. The first stage, known as the Acute Stage, occurs 1–2 months after transmission and is characterized by fever, depression, and generalized lymphadenopathy. The second stage, the Subclinical Stage, lasts from 4 weeks to several months after transmission. During this stage, symptoms decrease or disappear, but all infected cats remain viremic for life. The third stage, the Chronic Stage, involves the eventual onset of chronic infections due to immune system suppression. In this stage, cats may develop conditions such as stomatitis, odontoclasia, periodontitis, gingivitis, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, pneumonitis, enteritis, and dermatitis. FIV also infects other feline species and is endemic in some large wild cats, such as African lions. Unlike domestic cats, these wild species often do not exhibit symptoms, possibly due to evolutionary mutations that provide resistance to the virus.
